questions.question: A 21-months old child has discitis.

parts.text: Name two most common pathogens, to species level.
Why is discitis uncommon after age 7?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 most common pathogens (species level): Kingella kingae and Staphylococcus aureus.
b) Discitis is uncommon after age 7 because the intervertebral disc in young children is supplied by small transphyseal blood vessels that cross the cartilaginous vertebral endplate directly into the disc; this vascular supply normally regresses/involutes by around age 7-8 years, after which the disc becomes avascular, removing the hematogenous route by which organisms seed the disc space.

questions.question: Osteomyelitis in a 14mo, immunized. +/- septic arthritis.

parts.text: What time frame should you see changes on x-ray?
What are 2 changes you see on x-ray?
You aspirate the joint- purulent aspirate. What is the most likely org?
As per the latest CPS guidelines, what is the shortest duration of tx for this pt?

questions.model_answer:
a) Timeframe for radiographic changes: approximately 10-14 days (up to 2-3 weeks) after symptom onset; plain films are usually normal early in the disease course.
b) 2 x-ray changes: (1) periosteal reaction/elevation; (2) osteolysis/lucency (bony destruction).
c) Most likely organism from a purulent joint aspirate in a fully immunized 14-month-old: Staphylococcus aureus (Kingella kingae is also common in this age group and increasingly recognized with modern PCR-based detection).
d) Shortest duration per latest CPS guidance: approximately 3 weeks (20 days) total duration of therapy for uncomplicated osteomyelitis with good clinical response, transitioning to oral therapy early once clinically improving (septic arthritis alone can be treated even shorter, around 2-3 weeks).
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian Paediatric Society (CPS) statement on duration of therapy for pediatric osteoarticular infections.

parts.text: What is the timeline for acute osteomyelitis to show up on x-ray?

What is the most common pathogen in this scenario? Which antibiotic would you use to treat it?
What is the duration of treatment?

cohort_answer.text: X-ray changes seen 7-21 days after onset of symptoms: Lytic lesions and localized periosteal lifting. 'Current data support both the probability that K kingae is the dominant pathogen in children younger than 4 years old presenting with SA (with or without OA) and that S aureus is the more common pathogen in older children' (CPS statement osteoarticular infections). Treatment: Cefazolin followed by cephalexin oral stepdown when clinically improved, afebrile and CRP reduction 50%. Duration: 3-4 weeks depending on clinical response

questions.question: 21 month old with discitis

parts.text: Name the 2 most common organisms implicated in disease
Why do children >7 years of age rarely get discitis?

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 most common organisms: Kingella kingae and Staphylococcus aureus.
b) Children >7 years rarely get discitis because the transphyseal vessels supplying the avascular intervertebral disc in young children (which allow hematogenous seeding) regress and involute with age, so by around age 7-8 the disc is avascular and no longer accessible to hematogenous spread of infection.

parts.text: 2 most likely pathogens to cover with empiric therapy

cohort_answer.text: Uncommon (1-2 cases/30,000 visits, 6 and younger). Age <4 months: S. aureus, GBS, enteric gram negative. 4 months to adult: S. aureus, GAS, S. pneumo (enteric GNB uncommon). Increasing recognition of K. kingae in children <4 years. Salmonella. Empiric treatment for Kingella and SA (CTX and vanco) or cefazolin. Duration minimum 3-4 weeks

questions.question: PM Q22. Diabetic foot 2 cm ulcer, non-healing, recently treated with PO cephalexin but not improved

parts.text: a) Name 4 guideline recommended management that should be performed.
b) diagnostic tests
c) What is not covered with Keflex?
d) What 4 bacterial groups / types (use specific pathogen names if relevant or pathogen group if not) guide empiric therapy?

cohort_answer.text:
Glycemic control; wound care; offloading; vascular assessment; evaluation for osteomyelitis. Assess wound severity (mild/mod/severe); rule out osteomyelitis (probe the bone +/- XR); assess blood supply/PVD/venous insufficiency (pulses, AB index, +/- CT angio); address biomechanical problems and peripheral neuropathy; rule out resistant organisms
ABI, XR or MRI, deep tissue cultures after debridement to rule out resistant organisms/anaerobes, +/- bone bx
MRSA, Pseudomonas, anaerobes, resistant GNB and other GP
Pseudomonas, anaerobes, MRSA, GNB

parts.text: When will you see X-ray changes?
What are the 2 most common X-ray changes?
Most common bug and necessary treatment?
Duration?

cohort_answer.text: X-ray changes: soft tissue swelling at 3 days; lytic lesions, periosteal elevation, periosteal new bone formation at 10-20 days (7-21 days per CPS); sclerosis of bone after a month. Most common changes: periosteal reaction (new bone formation) and periosteal elevation (suggests abscess). Bug/treatment: Staph aureus (MSSA or MRSA depending on local epidemiology), Cloxacillin or Cefazolin for MSSA, Vancomycin for MRSA. Duration: 3-6 weeks (septic arthritis 3 weeks minimum, OM 4-6 weeks); uncomplicated AO/SA generally 3-4 weeks (4-6 weeks for hip SA).

parts.text: A) Why is discitis not as commonly seen in kids older than 7?
B) What are the 2 most common organisms to which antibiotic tx should be tailored?

cohort_answer.text:
Unlike adults, intervertebral disc in children is richly vascularized (vessels across cartilaginous vertebral plate into ring). After age 8 these vessels disappear but a rich anastomotic network remains peripherally. Rich vasculature <7 years enables bacterial emboli deposition within disc with possible extension to endplates/vertebral bodies
S. aureus; Kingella kingae

parts.text: List two most common organisms that empiric antibiotic should cover
Why is discitis much more uncommon in older children age >7 years?

cohort_answer.text: Staph aureus, Kingella kingae (<4). More opportunity for hematogenous seeding during systemic illness due to more vascular supply. Blood vessels are present in the cartilaginous vertebral endplate until ~7 years of age therefore disc infection occurs first rather than bone.

parts.text: B) What antibiotics to treat MRSA of spine?

cohort_answer.text:
S. aureus; Kingella kingae (less than 4 years, usually under 2)
Children more commonly colonized with Kingella in posterior pharynx - can lead to discitis/OM especially during respiratory infections. Intervertebral discs highly vascularized in children, easily hematogenously seeded. Blood vessels present in cartilaginous vertebral endplate until ~7 years, causing disc infection first rather than bone; after 10 years vessels obliterated
